subject: ventures/dynamodb-capacity-mode-advisor
professional: a senior AWS FinOps / cloud cost engineer who sets DynamoDB capacity modes for production tables; first checks: are the unit prices the current list prices (after the 2024-11-01 on-demand cut), is the RCU/WCU-hour vs per-million arithmetic and the break-even right, does the provisioned model include autoscaling headroom and the 1-unit floor, what happens with real CloudWatch exports (missing datapoints, 5-minute periods), and are GSIs, free tier and reserved capacity in or out of scope

evidence.correctness: Compared against AWS's own published price list, fetched live: `curl -sSL https://b0.p.awsstatic.com/pricing/2.0/meteredUnitMaps/dynamodb/USD/current/dynamodb.json` (gzip) gives US East (N. Virginia) 'PayPerRequest Read Request Units' 0.000000125, 'PayPerRequest Write Request Units' 0.000000625, 'Provisioned Read Units' 0.00013, 'Provisioned Write Units' 0.00065 = engine.mjs DEFAULT_PRICES $0.125/M, $0.625/M, $0.00013, $0.00065 (the post-2024-11-01 halved on-demand price; the pre-cut $0.25/$1.25 would put break-even at 14.4%, not 29%). aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/on-demand/ and /provisioned/ (HTTP 200) quote the same figures in their worked examples. Recomputed: (1) break-even 0.00013/(3600 x 0.125e-6) = 0.2889 for reads and 0.00065/(3600 x 0.625e-6) = 0.2889 for writes = CLI '~29%'. (2) Hand case, 168 h flat 100 RCU/s and 10 WCU/s: on-demand 100x3600x730/1e6x0.125 + 10x3600x730/1e6x0.625 = 32.85+16.425 = $49.275; autoscaled ceil(100/0.7)=143 RCU x 0.00013 x 730 + ceil(10/0.7)=15 WCU x 0.00065 x 730 = $20.688; CLI 49.275 / 20.688 exact. Fixed peak: hand ceil(100x1.1)=110 RCU, CLI 111 (JS 100*1.1 = 110.00000000000001), $15.75 vs $15.66: off by one unit from float. (3) Own Python (scratchpad dynamodb/indep.py) on the fixture week: on-demand $48.89, autoscaled $22.10, fixed peak $35.87 at 188/38 units = CLI. (4) eu-west-1 prices from the same AWS file (0.1415/M, 0.705/M, 0.000147, 0.000735) via --prices: on-demand $55.245, my Python $55.245; break-even 28.86%/28.96%. Not 4: the arithmetic is right for complete hourly rows, but rows are counted, not timed, so a CloudWatch export with missing (zero-traffic) periods or 5-minute Sums at the default period gives silently wrong monthly figures (see domain).
evidence.completeness: Walked every README/page feature: `node cli.mjs analyze fixtures/consumed-capacity.csv` (exit 0, 2 warnings), --json, --prices (file and bad file), --period 300, --current-rcu/--current-wcu (throttle error exit 1, pairing enforced exit 2), --fail-on warn (exit 1), stdin '-', --help, unknown option exit 2; all 8 rules fire on suitable input. Page in headless Chrome (Playwright, 375 px): 'Load worked example' renders the same $48.89/$22.10/$35.87 table and both warnings, scrollWidth 375, no console errors, no requests off localhost, opt-out button present. Docs page linked both ways, sitemap complete. No stubs or TODOs. Gaps: the page has no price editor (CLI only, the page says so).
evidence.verification: `node --test '*.test.mjs'`: 30 pass, 0 fail, ~150 ms. Tests check the on-demand formula, break-even, the mode direction on flat/idle/spiky input, throttling and CLI exit codes. Seeded 8 mutants with quality_mutate.py: 3 caught (730 -> 720 hours, fixed-peak cost scaled by sample hours, spiky threshold 6 -> 60), 5 survived: write capacity priced at the RCU rate (5x under-pricing of writes), autoscaling sized on the current period only (lag model removed), fixed-peak headroom removed, throttle test loosened to 1.5x current, and the 20% switch threshold dropped to 0. No test asserts an autoscaled or fixed-peak dollar figure.
evidence.craft: Read engine.mjs (167 lines), cli.mjs, usage.mjs, index.html script, all four test files. One engine shared by CLI and page (served engine.mjs byte-identical to source), zero dependencies, clear separation of parse/analyze/summarize, honest comments about the model. Defects: Math.ceil(peak*1.1) over-counts by one unit on exact multiples (float); a --prices file with a typo'd key is silently ignored and a non-numeric value prints '$NaN' and then recommends on-demand because NaN never wins the min; timestamps are parsed but never used (no ordering, gap or period check); the header detection treats any first non-numeric row naming read/write as a header.
evidence.claims: Checked 9 claims. Backed: us-east-1 list prices (AWS price list file, above); '29% break-even' (recomputed); docs '3.5 times' (1/0.2889 = 3.46); docs 'a perfectly steady table ... costs roughly 40% of on-demand' (hand case 20.69/49.28 = 42%); 'no network call / never uploaded' (Playwright request log empty off-origin, no fetch in engine/cli); usage counted only in localStorage with DNT/GPC honoured (usage.mjs:34); no-warranty and limits on page, docs and README; served llms.txt uses marisstella.app (`node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs` clean, live https://marisstella.app/dynamodb-capacity-mode-advisor/llms.txt fetched). Weak: docs 'daytime-heavy traffic with autoscaling usually lands in the 40-60% range' is unsourced (the shipped fixture itself lands at 64%); the limits list (free tier, reserved, Standard-IA, region, global tables, backups) omits GSIs and missing datapoints, the two a FinOps engineer would hit.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job: export a week of ConsumedRead/WriteCapacityUnits, paste, decide whether to switch. The answer for a fully active table is right and arrives in seconds with no AWS access. Gaps: the documented `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics` route returns two JSON documents the user must reshape by hand into three columns; GSIs (separate metrics, billed in the same mode) are not priced, so a write-heavy table with indexes is under-priced on both sides; a table on provisioned-with-autoscaling today can only be described as a fixed current RCU/WCU; idle hours missing from the export flip the answer for exactly the low-utilisation tables where on-demand should win.
evidence.domain: Compared against AWS DynamoDB pricing (price list file and pricing pages, fetched 2026-11-19) and DynamoDB/Application Auto Scaling behaviour as documented by AWS. Matches: current prices, RCU/WCU-hour vs request-unit equivalence, 1-unit provisioned floor, 70% default target-tracking, break-even and its equality for reads/writes, burst and autoscaling lag flagged. Departures: (a) the window is count x period, not the timestamp span; CloudWatch returns no datapoint for a period in which DynamoDB published no consumed-capacity value, so idle hours drop out of a real export, the 730 h extrapolation inflates on-demand and the provisioned modes lose their idle-hour cost: a 168 h week with 8 idle hours a day priced $65.70 on-demand / $28.90 autoscaled with zeros present, $98.55 / $31.41 (and a different 'cheapest mode') with those rows absent as CloudWatch would return them; (b) the period is not inferred from timestamps, so 5-minute Sums at the default 3600 s are priced 12x low ($4.11 vs $49.27) with no warning; (c) GSIs not modelled or mentioned; (d) autoscaling scale-in delay (15-minute alarms) and the daily decrease limit are not modelled, so the autoscaled figure is a lower bound (the page says it is a screen). Free tier and reserved capacity are out of scope and say so.

defects.what: The analysis window is row count x period (hours = count * periodSeconds / 3600), not the timestamp span. CloudWatch omits periods with no published datapoint, so idle hours drop out of a real export: on-demand is extrapolated from busy hours only and provisioned loses the idle-hour cost. A week with 8 idle hours a day goes from on-demand $65.70 / cheapest autoscaled to $98.55 / cheapest fixed peak when the zero rows are absent. Low-utilisation tables, where on-demand should win, are the ones most affected
The period is never inferred or checked from the timestamps: 5-minute Sums pasted at the default 3600 s are priced 12x low (on-demand $4.11 vs $49.27) with no warning

Tests would not catch pricing bugs in the provisioned modes: 5 of 8 mutants survive, including writes priced at the RCU rate (5x under-pricing of WCU), the autoscaling lag model removed, fixed-peak headroom removed, the throttle test loosened 1.5x and the 20% switch threshold dropped; no test asserts an autoscaled or fixed-peak dollar figure

Global secondary indexes are neither priced nor listed as a limit; their consumed capacity is a separate CloudWatch dimension billed in the table's capacity mode, so a table with write-heavy GSIs is under-priced in every mode and the limits list on page and README is incomplete
Fixed-peak units use Math.ceil(peak * 1.1) on a float: 100 RCU/s gives 111 (100*1.1 = 110.00000000000001), 200 gives 221, one unit too many on exact multiples
--prices is not validated: an unknown key is silently ignored and a non-numeric value prints '$NaN' for both provisioned modes and then reports on-demand as cheapest, exit 0
Docs page says daytime-heavy traffic with autoscaling 'usually lands in the 40-60% range' with no source; the shipped fixture itself lands at 64%

verdict: A small, honest screen whose arithmetic is right: its default prices equal AWS's live us-east-1 price list (the post-November-2024 $0.125/$0.625 per million on-demand and $0.00013/$0.00065 per unit-hour provisioned), the 29% break-even and the docs page's 3.5x and ~40% ratios recompute, and a hand case, my own Python on the fixture and eu-west-1 prices from AWS's file all match the CLI to the cent (fixed peak aside, one unit high from a float ceiling). The page and CLI do everything they claim, with nothing uploaded. It misses the bar on verification and domain: the monthly window comes from the row count, so a real CloudWatch export with missing idle periods inflates on-demand by 50% and can flip the recommended mode, 5-minute data at the default period is priced 12x low without a warning, GSIs are not mentioned, and 5 of 8 seeded bugs (writes priced at the read rate among them) survive the 30 tests. A FinOps engineer would trust it on a fully active table with complete hourly rows, not on the idle or indexed tables where the decision matters most.
